WEEKLY MEETINGS
RICK JAMES
One of the most effective means of evangelism on
campus is for students to invite their friends to an
evangelistic talk or event—provided, of course, that
the event is done well. The problem is that it’s typically
not in the campus budget to bring in an evangelistic
speaker. The solution is to do it yourself. Take the
points, content, and approaches used by evangelistic
speakers and do the talk yourself. Show some
interesting video clips, hijack their data and research,
and follow the outline of their presentation. No, it
will probably not be as good, but it is both cheap and
effective.
Here are a handful of my evangelistic talk outlines,
feel free to pillage. But if you don’t use these, still think
in terms of doing a low-cost version of existing outreach
topics and talks.
E VA N G E L I S T I C W E E K LY M E E T I N G S 1
While this will save you some money, the bigger
reason for this approach is so that you can have
multiple evangelistic meetings over the course of
the year. Ideally, every six weeks or so your meeting
should be something that students can invite their non-
Christian friends to.
As you’ll see from the following outlines, events on
the calendar provide great opportunities for outreach
topics.

Valentines Day provides an opportunity to reach out
to the campus on the topic of relationship/sex/dating.
What follows is an interesting way to get at that

BULIMIC RELATIONSHIPS
In the disease of bulimia the person longs for the
taste of food, but they don’t want what comes with it,
weight, nutrition, and calories. So they have developed
a gag reflex that allows them to taste the food while
avoiding a commitment to its digestion.
INTRODUCTION
Begin with some great clip from a romantic comedy.
Explain you are far from an expert and back that up by
sharing a humiliating dating/marriage story.
Example: have you ever known someone that enjoys

talk of marriage and long term commitment, they say,
“excuse me, I need to go to the bathroom, blechhhh.”
They have a gag reflex to commitment. They love the
taste of a relationship but there’s no way they’re going
to swallow it.

It seems that in most of the horror movies that I’ve
watched, someone uncovers some dusty old scroll that
contains the secrets of possession and the hidden art
of exorcism, apparently cloistered in some monastery
for a millennia or two. So I surveyed of some of the
ancient literature of the early Christian Church
(c.100-400 AD) to see what I might uncover on the
subject of demonic possession.
Methodius (c. 260 AD) seems to be the first to
mention the practice of ongoing exorcisms by the
Church. Tertullian (c. early third century) indicates
that the “power (of exorcism) should be taken
seriously and not exercised indiscriminately.” Saint
Augustine notes that the binding of Satan was
accomplished through Jesus’ invasion of Satan’s
territory on earth, but that there were “continuing
acts of binding (exorcism) that were still taking place.”
In summary the creepy old scrolls (actually they’re
available in most libraries) tell us very little and
give us no eyewitness accounts of possession or
exorcism. What I did find of interest was that the
practice of exorcism has changed very little in the
last two thousand years, at least within the Catholic
Church. The Roman Exorcism Ritual that is still used
today, dates back to the second century and has not
been significantly altered in 1,6000 years. I guess the
position of the Church is “if it works don’t mess with
it.”
